results.title: Laudation for Seyla Benhabib: Introduction to the Adorno Prize Lecture—Frankfurt, September 11, 2024
results.abstract: As a female political philosopher, born in Turkey to a Sephardic Jewish family, educated in America and Germany, and enjoying an illustrious teaching career in the United States, Seyla Benhabib has long pondered the limits placed on the validity of transcendent ideas by their contextual genesis. This “laudatio” for the Adorno Prize she was awarded in 2024 by the city of Frankfurt examines her work, with its special debts to Habermas and Arendt, as an evolving attempt to explore this issue with special reference to the challenges of feminism, postcolonial anti-Eurocentrism, the populist assault on democracy, and the global refugee crisis. Her defense of cosmopolitan ideals against ethnonationalism and abstract universalism shows that transcendent ideas can have particular genetic origins.

results.title: The Phantom of Liberty: Mo(der)nism and Postcolonial Imaginations in India
Defending Reason
results.abstract: This chapter provides a postcolonial critique of those defenders of a universal and singular Reason who, forced to acknowledge that modern knowledge has been shaped by its historical and cultural contexts, nonetheless seek to provide reasons why the presuppositions undergirding the social sciences have a claim to transhistorical and transcultural validity. Engaging in detail with the defenses of Reason mounted by Jürgen Habermas, Karl-Otto Apel, and John Rawls, it argues that these are not persuasive because they presuppose that which they seek to validate or “ground.” It concludes that modern knowledge is a historically and culturally specific way of knowing and being in the world, that there are good reasons to doubt that it transcends these particularities, and that while modern Western knowledge has become global, that does not validate the claim that it is universal.
